title: HTML Tags Proposed
epigraph: A simple language for linking documents across a global network.
body: Tim Berners-Lee outlined eleven elements to describe structure and reference. The proposal carried no fees and claimed no patent.
The memo circulated through CERN's internal networks, unseen by the outside world.
doc: The original 1990 proposal described HTML as a markup language for hypertext. Eleven tags were sufficient to link any document anywhere.
question: How many tags did the original HTML specification include?
clue: eleven elements to describe structure and reference

title: HTTP Request Laid Down
epigraph: The first command sent across a socket would change communication forever.
body: A GET request traveled from one machine to another with no body, only a path. The server replied with text that appeared on a screen.
No one predicted the method would outlive the laboratory where it was born.
doc: The first HTTP specification defined methods for retrieving resources. GET was the method that started it all, returning stateless text to the caller.
question: What HTTP method was defined in the first specification?
clue: The first method defined was GET

title: Browser Without Pictures
epigraph: Text reigned until an image tag proved the world was ready for more.
body: The first browser rendered only fonts and whitespace. Tables arranged layout. Images required a separate viewer and appeared as placeholders.
The world grew accustomed to reading before it learned to see.
doc: Early 1990s browsers prioritized text delivery. The IMG element was added mid-1993 after the initial proposal, changing visual communication forever.
question: What did early browsers render before images were supported?

title: CERN Server Room Cooling
epigraph: Machines generated heat that the room could not tolerate indefinitely.
body: The first web server filled a rack and hummed day and night. Operators monitored temperature on a dial that crept upward.
The building's ventilation system struggled to keep the prototypes from overheating during long debugging sessions.
doc: The original web server ran nonstop from late 1990 through 1993. Hardware ran warm, but the idea ran hotter, spreading through corridors and across continents.
question: What problem did the first web server hardware face?
clue: Operators monitored temperature on a dial

title: NeXT Step Toward the Web
epigraph: A different computer architecture carried the idea beyond the laboratory walls.
body: Tim Berners-Lee used a NeXT workstation to build the first browser and server. The object-oriented environment made the code easier to shape and reshape.
The purple-hued screen became a familiar sight in the early days of the web.
doc: NeXT computers provided the development platform for the first web tools. The combination of Objective-C and Unix made the early code portable and extensible.
question: What computer did Tim Berners-Lee use to build the first web tools?

title: First Web Address Book
epigraph: Names translated to numbers in a directory no one expected to need.
body: Before DNS was universal, numeric addresses connected early adopters. A text file mapped names to numbers, updated by hand each month.
The list grew quietly as more hosts came online, each entry a pact between administrator and user.
doc: The early internet used HOSTS.TXT files distributed by Stanford Research Institute. Before the domain name system, every computer knew its numeric address by heart.
question: What system mapped names to numbers before DNS existed?

title: Markup Language Compromise
epigraph: What looked like chaos to some was structure to others.
body: The HTML proposal borrowed from SGML but stripped away complexity. The result was a minimal syntax that could be parsed by hand or by machine.
Purists wanted full SGML compliance. Practitioners wanted to get pages up by Friday.
doc: HTML was designed to be a simplified subset of SGML. The compromise meant fewer rules, easier authoring, and faster adoption across heterogeneous hardware.
question: What did HTML simplify from SGML?

title: Link Rot Already Beginning
epigraph: Addresses change, and the web remembers only what is copied anew.
body: Early page authors discovered that links broke when machines were taken offline. The practice of quoting sources became essential, not optional.
Mailing lists preserved discussions, but the original URLs faded into silence.
doc: The ephemeral nature of early network addresses meant that link rot appeared within months of publication. Archival effort was required to preserve the first generation of web content.
question: What problem did early page authors face with links?
clue: Links broke when machines were taken offline

title: CERN Public Announcement 1991
epigraph: A note posted to a newsgroup reached beyond the laboratory fence.
body: In 1991 the web was declared free for all. A posting to alt.hypertext announced the software and invited collaboration.
The response came from universities and research centers worldwide, each asking how they could join.
doc: CERN placed the web software in the public domain on April 30, 1993. The 1991 newsgroup post marked the first public invitation to use and improve the system.
question: What newsgroup carried the first public web announcement?
clue: Posting to alt.hypertext announced the software

title: Line-Mode Browser Debut
epigraph: The first browser to run anywhere, not just on a workstation.
body: The Line-Mode Browser rendered HTML on terminals without a graphical display. Users typed URLs and read structured text on dumb terminals across the network.
Portability mattered more than prettiness. The browser proved the web could reach any connected device.
doc: Written in C by Tim Berners-Lee and Nicola Pellow, the Line-Mode Browser was the first publicly available web browser. It ran on any system with a TCP stack, expanding the web beyond workstations and research labs.
question: What allowed the Line-Mode Browser to run on any connected device?
clue: Ran on any system with a TCP stack
